title: The Open Boat

teacherSummary.text: After a steamer sinks, four men, the injured captain, the cook, the oiler Billie and the correspondent, row a ten-foot dinghy for thirty hours off the Florida coast. They see land and a lifesaving station, but no one comes. Taking turns at the oars, they form a quiet brotherhood. At last they run the surf; the oiler, the strongest, drowns. The survivors feel they can now be 'interpreters' of the sea's voice.

annotationFocus.passage: The injured captain, lying in the bow, was at this time buried in that profound dejection and indifference which comes, temporarily at least, to even the bravest and most enduring when, willy nilly, the firm fails, the army loses, the ship goes down. The mind of the master of a vessel is rooted deep in the timbers of her, though he command for a day or a decade, and this captain had on him the stern impression of a scene in the grays of dawn of seven turned faces, and later a stump of a top-mast with a white ball on it that slashed to and fro at the waves, went low and lower, and down. Thereafter there was something strange in his voice. Although steady, it was deep with mourning, and of a quality beyond oration or tears.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “NONE of them knew the color of the sky” slowly and put it in my own words: The four shipwrecked men in the small boat never look up, so none of them knows the color of the sky. Next, craft. I notice the sentence opens with a capitalized "NONE," stressing that all of them, without exception, are absorbed. The strongest word is “NONE”: the capitals make the word land like a blow and include every man in the boat. Then, effect. Why does the story begin with what the men did not know? My answer: The story begins with what the men did not know because they could see only the waves that might kill them; Crane shows that survival narrows the men's whole world to the next few feet of water.
